figAlt: Timeline: September 2026, Uber leaves Nigeria. October 2026, Moove closes its Nigerian operations and hands around ₦35bn of vehicles to drivers. Annotated: plausible link, not established cause.
figCaption: Moove gave no reason, drivers could still work on other platforms such as Bolt, and Moove continues to raise capital elsewhere. Sources: Launch Base Africa (Sept 2026); Nation Africa (2026); Nairametrics (Oct 2026).
why: Moove’s 2026 exit from Nigeria is used as a comparator rather than a full case, because the seven dimensions were not applied to it. It financed ride-hailing drivers’ cars, with repayment linked to their platform earnings, and announced the end of its Nigerian operations about a month after Uber left Nigeria in September 2026, transferring vehicles valued at about ₦35bn to customers at no further cost (Nairametrics, October 2026; Nation Africa, 2026). The link to Uber’s exit is a plausible explanation rather than an established cause. Autogirl, by contrast, had no fleet debt to unwind.

quotes.label: From the synthesis (Section 06)
quotes.text: Moove suggests a second risk: debt suits a fleet, but repayment tied to one platform’s earnings is exposed to that platform’s presence in the market, so lender, customer and platform concentration can matter as much as the instrument.

quotes.label: Cautionary cases as a mirror
quotes.text: Moove used an instrument suited to vehicles, but its Nigerian repayments were linked to ride-hailing earnings, and it left Nigeria a month after Uber did; it gave no reason, and its business elsewhere continues to raise capital.

quotes.label: Framework rule (Section 07)
quotes.text: Avoid repayments that depend on a single outside platform (Moove).
